I live in North Montery county CA and our Falls are warmer than our Summers and a little drier too and my Purpureas often make more open hoods during the year except for Fall where they almost universally have them strongly folded inward then. My conclusion is that the hoods folding inward is a response to high temperatures and drier air and possibly less rainfall. Maybe the Montanas are more prone to do it. I'm not saying they are not but even my Roseas make strongly folded inward hoods in the Fall so I'm pretty sure it's primarily environmental.

posts.body_html:
HI Sunbelle-our night temps. here are in the mid 50's. It seems these purps. tend to color up for me during the fall, especially after the pitchers have aged a bit. They're starting to show some interesting veination right now.

This plant photographed below was given to my good friend, Rob Co, last winter. He grew it in his greenhouse-same latitude, same night temperatures, but his grow season is about 2 weeks ahead of mine. Notice his plant is also bigger than mine. In a greenhouse, when the weather outside is cold, it's warm in there, whereas outdoors, the plants stay cold. This delays a lot of growth ourdoors, and delays the "aging" of the traps. It seems when you have warm days every day in a greenhouse, you'll get faster growth and quicker maturity compared to outdoor growing.

FYI: One of those green plants photographed in the previous page is the exact same clone as Rob's plant below.

Photograph taken 6/16/13:






This thing is a beauty! After seeing this photo, does anyone still have suspicions on whether this is the real deal? Growing plants outdoors definitely brings out some different phenotypes that can be confusing even to the trained eye.
